910.name: Earliest Civilizations: Caral, Chavín, and Paracas
910.description: The foundational civilizations of ancient Peru — Caral-Supe (the oldest city in the Americas, c. 3000 BCE), the Chavín religious horizon, and the Paracas textile and medical traditions — establishing the Andean cultural trajectory.

sub_clusters.name: Caral-Supe: Oldest City in the Americas
sub_clusters.description: The Norte Chico/Caral-Supe civilization (c. 3000–1800 BCE) was the earliest known complex society in the Americas, contemporaneous with ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia. The city of Caral, with its monumental pyramids, sunken plazas, and quipu-like recording devices, developed without ceramics, writing, or warfare — a unique model of civilizational emergence based on maritime-agricultural exchange.
key_events: Caral flourishes as oldest city in the Americas — c. 3000 BCE
Caral-Supe designated UNESCO World Heritage Site — 2009

sub_clusters.name: Chavín and Paracas Cultural Horizons
sub_clusters.description: The Chavín culture (c. 900–200 BCE) — centred at Chavín de Huántar in the highlands — was the first pan-Andean religious horizon, spreading its jaguar-serpent-eagle iconography across a vast region. The contemporaneous Paracas culture on the southern coast produced extraordinary textiles and practised cranial surgery (trepanation) with remarkable survival rates.
key_events: Chavín de Huántar becomes major religious-ceremonial centre — c. 900 BCE
Paracas textile tradition reaches extraordinary sophistication

910.name: Regional Kingdoms: Nazca, Moche, Wari, and Chimú
910.description: The flourishing of Peru's great pre-Inca regional civilizations — the Nazca Lines, the Moche warrior-priests, the Wari empire, the Tiwanaku influence, and the Chimú kingdom — before the Inca consolidation.

sub_clusters.name: The Nazca Lines and Nazca Culture
sub_clusters.description: The Nazca culture of southern Peru's desert coast created the famous Nazca Lines — enormous geoglyphs (some over 300 metres long) depicting animals, plants, and geometric shapes visible only from the air. Their purpose remains debated: astronomical calendars, ritual pathways, or water-related ceremonies. Nazca also built impressive underground aqueducts (puquios) still in use today.
key_events: Nazca Lines created — c. 200 BCE–600 CE, UNESCO World Heritage Site
Nazca puquios (underground aqueducts) — engineering marvel still in use

sub_clusters.name: The Moche Civilization
sub_clusters.description: The Moche (c. 100–700 CE) of Peru's northern coast built massive adobe pyramids (Huacas del Sol y de la Luna), created some of the finest portrait ceramics in the ancient world, and practised elaborate warrior-priest rituals including human sacrifice. The discovery of the Lord of Sipán's tomb in 1987 was one of the greatest archaeological finds in the Americas.
key_events: Huaca del Sol — largest adobe structure in pre-Columbian Americas
Discovery of Lord of Sipán's tomb — 1987, 'King Tut of the Americas'

sub_clusters.name: Wari, Tiwanaku, and Chimú Empires
sub_clusters.description: The Wari Empire (c. 600–1000 CE) was the first Andean empire, establishing administrative centres and road networks across Peru that the Inca would later adopt. The Tiwanaku polity (centred near Lake Titicaca) influenced southern Peru. The Chimú kingdom (c. 900–1470) built Chan Chan — the largest adobe city in the world — and controlled 1,000 km of coastline before being conquered by the Inca.
key_events: Wari Empire establishes first Andean road and administrative network
Chan Chan built — largest adobe city in the world, Chimú capital

920.name: The Inca Empire: Tawantinsuyu
920.description: The rise, expansion, and zenith of the Inca Empire — Tawantinsuyu ('The Four Regions Together') — the largest empire in pre-Columbian Americas, stretching from Colombia to Chile, with its capital at Cusco and its iconic citadels, road systems, and administrative genius.

sub_clusters.name: Inca Origins and the Kingdom of Cusco
sub_clusters.description: The Inca began as a small kingdom in the Cusco valley, founded (according to legend) by Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, who emerged from Lake Titicaca. For two centuries, the Inca were one of many competing highland polities. Their dramatic expansion began under Pachacuti (1438), who defeated the powerful Chanka confederation and transformed the Inca from a regional kingdom into an imperial power.

sub_clusters.name: Imperial Expansion and Peak
sub_clusters.description: Under Pachacuti, Túpac Inca Yupanqui, and Huayna Cápac, the Inca conquered territory from southern Colombia to central Chile — approximately 12 million people across 2 million km². They built 40,000 km of roads (the Qhapaq Ñan), developed the quipu recording system, constructed Machu Picchu and Sacsayhuamán, and administered the empire through the mit'a labour tax, ayllu communities, and a redistributive economy without money or markets.
key_events: Pachacuti defeats the Chanka and begins Inca expansion — 1438
Construction of Machu Picchu — c. 1450
Inca Empire reaches peak extent under Huayna Cápac — c. 1527

sub_clusters.name: The Inca Civil War
sub_clusters.description: Huayna Cápac's death (c. 1527) — possibly from a smallpox epidemic that preceded European contact — triggered a devastating civil war between his sons Atahualpa (Quito-based) and Huáscar (Cusco-based). Atahualpa won, but the fratricidal conflict fatally weakened the empire just as Francisco Pizarro arrived on the coast.
key_events: Death of Huayna Cápac, possibly from smallpox — c. 1527
Atahualpa defeats Huáscar in civil war — 1532

930.name: The Spanish Conquest and Fall of the Inca
930.description: Francisco Pizarro's audacious conquest of the Inca Empire — the capture and execution of Atahualpa at Cajamarca, the fall of Cusco, the Spanish civil wars, and the destruction of the last Inca resistance at Vilcabamba.

sub_clusters.name: Cajamarca: The Capture of Atahualpa
sub_clusters.description: On November 16, 1532, Francisco Pizarro — with roughly 168 men — ambushed and captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in one of the most consequential events in world history. Atahualpa paid a legendary ransom (a room filled with gold and twice with silver) but was executed on July 26, 1533. The 'ambush at Cajamarca' has been endlessly debated as a case study in the collision of civilizations.
key_events: Pizarro captures Atahualpa at Cajamarca — November 16, 1532
Atahualpa's ransom room filled with gold and silver — 1533
Atahualpa executed — July 26, 1533

sub_clusters.name: The Fall of Cusco and the Neo-Inca State
sub_clusters.description: The Spanish entered Cusco in November 1533 and installed puppet Inca rulers. Manco Inca's Great Rebellion (1536) nearly expelled the Spanish but ultimately failed. Manco retreated to Vilcabamba, establishing a rump Neo-Inca state that resisted until Túpac Amaru I was captured and executed in Cusco's main plaza in 1572, ending the Inca royal line.
key_events: Manco Inca's Great Rebellion besieges Cusco — 1536
Túpac Amaru I executed in Cusco — 1572, end of Inca resistance

930.name: The Viceroyalty of Peru: Silver, Church, and Colonial Society
930.description: The Viceroyalty of Peru as the administrative heart of Spanish South America — the silver economy (Potosí), the colonial caste system, Lima as the 'City of Kings,' the Catholic Church's dominance, and the devastating demographic collapse of the indigenous population.

sub_clusters.name: Potosí, Silver, and the Colonial Economy
sub_clusters.description: The discovery of the Potosí silver mountain (1545, in modern Bolivia but then under Peru's viceroyalty) transformed the global economy. Potosí became one of the largest cities in the world, and Peruvian silver financed the Spanish Empire, fueled European inflation, and was traded as far as China. The colonial mit'a system forced indigenous men to work the mines under horrific conditions — an estimated 8 million people died in the Potosí mines over the colonial period.
key_events: Discovery of Potosí silver mountain — 1545
Lima established as capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru — 1542

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Lima: City of Kings
sub_clusters.description: Lima, founded by Pizarro in 1535 as 'La Ciudad de los Reyes,' became the wealthiest and most important city in Spanish South America — seat of the viceroy, the Inquisition, and the oldest university in the Americas (San Marcos, 1551). Colonial society was rigidly stratified by the sistema de castas — a racial hierarchy placing Spanish-born peninsulares at the top and indigenous and African peoples at the bottom.

sub_clusters.name: Indigenous Resistance and Túpac Amaru II
sub_clusters.description: Indigenous resistance to colonial exploitation culminated in the Great Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II (José Gabriel Condorcanqui, 1780–1783) — the largest anti-colonial uprising in the Americas before independence. Túpac Amaru II rallied 60,000+ indigenous followers before being captured and brutally executed in Cusco in 1781. The rebellion was suppressed with extreme violence but permanently weakened Spanish authority.
key_events: Juan Santos Atahualpa's rebellion in the jungle — 1742–1756
Túpac Amaru II rebellion — 1780–1783, largest anti-colonial uprising in the Americas
Túpac Amaru II executed in Cusco — May 18, 1781

940.name: Independence: San Martín, Bolívar, and the Birth of the Republic
940.description: Peru's complex path to independence — the last major Spanish stronghold in South America, liberated through the combined efforts of José de San Martín and Simón Bolívar — and the chaotic early republican period.

sub_clusters.name: San Martín and Bolívar: Liberation of Peru
sub_clusters.description: Peru, as the centre of Spanish power in South America, required liberation from outside. José de San Martín arrived from Chile (1820) and declared Peruvian independence on July 28, 1821, but could not defeat the Spanish militarily. Simón Bolívar arrived from the north (1823) and his lieutenant Antonio José de Sucre won the decisive Battle of Ayacucho on December 9, 1824 — the final major battle of South American independence.
key_events: San Martín declares Peruvian independence — July 28, 1821
Battle of Ayacucho — December 9, 1824, ends Spanish rule in South America
Bolívar governs Peru — 1824–1826

sub_clusters.name: Caudillo Era and the Early Republic
sub_clusters.description: The early republic was dominated by military caudillos competing for power, with chronic instability, coups, and constitutional rewrites. The Peru-Bolivia Confederation (1836–1839) under Andrés de Santa Cruz was opposed and destroyed by Chile and Argentine interests. The guano boom would eventually provide economic stability.

940.name: The Guano Age and the War of the Pacific
940.description: Peru's guano-fueled prosperity and reckless borrowing, the catastrophic War of the Pacific against Chile (1879–1884), national humiliation, and the difficult postwar reconstruction.

sub_clusters.name: The Guano Age: Boom and Bust
sub_clusters.description: Peru's vast guano deposits (bird droppings used as fertilizer) generated enormous wealth — guano revenues funded 80% of the government budget at their peak. President Ramón Castilla used guano income to abolish slavery (1854) and indigenous tribute, but subsequent governments squandered revenue through corruption and reckless foreign borrowing. Chinese indentured labourers (coolies) were brought to work the guano islands under brutal conditions.
key_events: Guano boom begins under President Castilla — 1845
Slavery abolished in Peru — 1854

sub_clusters.name: The War of the Pacific (1879–1884)
sub_clusters.description: The War of the Pacific (1879–1884) pitted Chile against Peru and Bolivia over nitrate-rich territories. Chile's superior naval and military forces captured Lima (January 1881), which was occupied and looted. Peru lost its wealthy southern province of Tarapacá, and the humiliating Treaty of Ancón (1883) ceded territory that defined Peru's sense of national grievance for generations.
key_events: War of the Pacific begins — April 1879
Chilean forces capture and occupy Lima — January 1881
Treaty of Ancón — Peru cedes Tarapacá to Chile — 1883

sub_clusters.name: Postwar Reconstruction and the Aristocratic Republic
sub_clusters.description: Post-war Peru underwent painful reconstruction. The Grace Contract (1889) settled foreign debts by handing railways and guano rights to British creditors. The 'Aristocratic Republic' (1895–1919) was an oligarchic period dominated by coastal landed elites, banking interests, and export agriculture (sugar, cotton), while the indigenous highland majority remained marginalized.

950.name: Reform, Revolution, and Military Government
950.description: Peru's turbulent 20th century — APRA and the populist challenge, the rise of indigenous consciousness, Velasco's radical military revolution, and the cycles of democratic and authoritarian rule that defined the era.

sub_clusters.name: APRA, Oligarchy, and Political Conflict
sub_clusters.description: Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre founded APRA (1924), Latin America's first mass-based populist party, which the military and oligarchy blocked from power for decades. The Leguía oncenio (1919–1930) modernized Lima but repressed opposition. José Carlos Mariátegui introduced Marxist analysis of Peru's indigenous 'problem.' The cycle of civilian-military alternation continued through mid-century.
key_events: Haya de la Torre founds APRA — 1924
Mariátegui publishes 'Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality' — 1928

sub_clusters.name: Velasco's Revolutionary Military Government
sub_clusters.description: General Juan Velasco Alvarado's military coup (1968) launched the most radical left-wing military government in Latin American history — implementing sweeping agrarian reform (breaking up haciendas), nationalizing the oil industry (expelling IPC), recognizing Quechua as an official language, and attempting to reshape Peruvian society. The revolution was reversed after 1975 under the more conservative General Morales Bermúdez, and the military returned power to civilians in 1980.
key_events: Velasco's coup begins revolutionary military government — October 3, 1968
Agrarian Reform Law breaks up haciendas — 1969
Quechua recognized as official language — 1975

950.name: Sendero Luminoso, MRTA, and the Internal Conflict
950.description: Peru's devastating internal armed conflict (1980–2000) — the Maoist Sendero Luminoso (Shining Path), the MRTA, state counterinsurgency violence, and the estimated 69,000 dead — mostly indigenous Quechua speakers in the highlands.

sub_clusters.name: The Rise of Sendero Luminoso
sub_clusters.description: Abimael Guzmán ('Presidente Gonzalo') launched Sendero Luminoso's Maoist insurgency from Ayacucho in 1980. The movement's extreme violence — targeting peasants, local officials, and rival leftists as much as the state — and the equally brutal military counterinsurgency devastated the highlands. The MRTA (Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement) operated separately in the jungle and urban areas. An estimated 69,000 people died, 75% of them Quechua-speaking indigenous civilians.
key_events: Sendero Luminoso begins armed struggle in Ayacucho — May 1980
Capture of Abimael Guzmán — September 12, 1992

sub_clusters.name: Truth Commission and National Reckoning
sub_clusters.description: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (CVR, 2001–2003) documented the conflict's devastating toll: 69,280 estimated deaths and disappearances. The Commission assigned responsibility to Sendero Luminoso (54%), the military and security forces (37%), and other armed groups. The finding that 75% of victims were Quechua-speaking indigenous people exposed the deep racial and social fractures in Peruvian society.

960.name: The Fujimori Era: Authoritarianism and Economic Reform
960.description: Alberto Fujimori's decade in power — neoliberal economic shock therapy, the autogolpe (self-coup), defeat of Sendero Luminoso, the Japanese Embassy hostage crisis, forced sterilizations, corruption, and eventual flight and conviction.

sub_clusters.name: Fujimori, the Autogolpe, and Neoliberal Reforms
sub_clusters.description: Alberto Fujimori — the son of Japanese immigrants — won the 1990 election and implemented 'Fujishock' economic reforms that tamed hyperinflation but devastated the poor. His 1992 autogolpe (self-coup) dissolved Congress and rewrote the constitution. His intelligence chief Vladimiro Montesinos ran a vast corruption and surveillance network. Fujimori's forced sterilization programme targeted 300,000+ indigenous women. He fled to Japan in 2000 and was later extradited, convicted, and sentenced to 25 years for human rights abuses and corruption.
key_events: Fujimori elected president — 1990
Autogolpe (self-coup) — April 5, 1992
Japanese Embassy hostage crisis (MRTA) — December 1996 – April 1997
Fujimori convicted of human rights crimes — 2009

960.name: Democratic Instability and Contemporary Peru
960.description: Post-Fujimori Peru's chronic political instability — revolving-door presidents, endemic corruption (Odebrecht scandal), the Pedro Castillo crisis, persistent inequality, and the tension between Lima and the provinces.

sub_clusters.name: The Revolving-Door Presidency
sub_clusters.description: Peru cycled through six presidents in five years (2018–2023) — a record of instability. Toledo, García (who died by suicide facing arrest), Humala, Kuczynski, Vizcarra, Merino, Sagasti, Castillo, and Boluarte all faced corruption charges, impeachment, or removal. Pedro Castillo's attempted self-coup (December 2022) and arrest marked a new nadir. Every living former president has been investigated, charged, or convicted of corruption.
key_events: Pedro Castillo's attempted self-coup and arrest — December 7, 2022
Dina Boluarte becomes first female president — December 2022
Odebrecht corruption scandal implicates multiple presidents

sub_clusters.name: Economic Growth and Persistent Inequality
sub_clusters.description: Peru experienced strong economic growth (2002–2013), driven by mining (copper, gold), agro-exports, and services, lifting millions out of poverty. However, deep inequality persists between coastal Lima and the highland/jungle provinces, between Spanish-speaking mestizo elites and Quechua/Aymara indigenous communities, and between the formal and informal economies. COVID-19 hit Peru harder than almost any country — the world's highest per-capita death rate.

sub_clusters.name: Cultural Heritage, Tourism, and National Identity
sub_clusters.description: Peru's extraordinary archaeological and cultural heritage — Machu Picchu (voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World, 2007), Cusco, the Nazca Lines, and Amazonian biodiversity — drives a major tourism industry. Peruvian cuisine (ceviche, gastronomy boom) has gained global recognition. The tension between commercial exploitation and indigenous rights over cultural patrimony remains ongoing.
key_events: Machu Picchu voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World — 2007
Peru's gastronomic boom gains global recognition

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
